modules.title: C++ Foundations
modules.description: Learn c++ foundations through explanations, examples, and practical exercises.

topics.title: Overview
topics.description: Understand the C++ language, its programming styles, core ecosystem, and the mental model needed for writing reliable programs.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
C++ is easiest to understand when you separate three layers: the language rules, the standard library, and the toolchain that turns source code into a running program. The language gives you types, expressions, classes, templates, object lifetime, and control flow. The library gives you ready-made facilities such as strings, containers, algorithms, streams, smart pointers, and time utilities. The compiler and linker turn those pieces into executable machine code.

C++ also supports several styles at once. Procedural code is useful for straightforward transformations, object-oriented design is useful when state and invariants belong together, and generic programming is useful when the same algorithm should work with many types. Good C++ design is not about using every feature; it is about choosing the smallest abstraction that makes the program clear and safe.

A strong beginner mental model is to ask four questions for every program: What data exists? Who owns that data? What operations are allowed? How long does each object remain valid? These questions become increasingly important as you move from simple variables to classes, dynamic resources, templates, and concurrency.

A useful way to make this model concrete is to follow one value through the whole program. A value starts with a type, is stored in an object, is passed through expressions or functions, and eventually reaches an output or another component. The compiler uses the type information to reject many invalid operations before the program runs, while runtime behavior still depends on object lifetime, resource ownership, and program logic. C++ therefore rewards deliberate design rather than treating syntax as the main goal.

The language also gives programmers choices that have different costs. A direct value is often simpler than a pointer, a standard container is usually safer than manual allocation, and a small class can be preferable to a large inheritance hierarchy. Learning C++ means learning these trade-offs gradually. Start with values and functions, then introduce references, classes, templates, and lower-level facilities when the problem actually benefits from them.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use this foundation to decide whether a problem is best represented with functions, classes, templates, or a combination of them.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain the difference between the C++ language, standard library, compiler, and linker. Be able to compare procedural, object-oriented, and generic programming without claiming that one style is universally best. A strong answer also mentions object lifetime, ownership, RAII, and why modern C++ favors standard-library facilities over unnecessary manual resource management.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Treating C++ as only an object-oriented language, assuming source code is executed directly, or assuming every platform has identical type sizes. Another common mistake is jumping to raw pointers and manual allocation before understanding values, containers, and object lifetime.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Read a C++ program as a set of typed objects moving through well-defined lifetimes. For every important object, ask what creates it, who owns its resources, how it is accessed, and when destruction occurs. This mental model connects beginner syntax to later topics such as references, smart pointers, move semantics, templates, and concurrency.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: You are learning C++ as a systems language and need one mental model connecting source code, the standard library, compilation, object lifetime, and resource ownership.
Avoid: Treating C++ as “C with classes” or assuming the language automatically manages every resource. The central skill is controlling lifetime and expressing ownership clearly.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A service may use `std::vector` for storage, RAII wrappers for sockets/files/locks, and interfaces for replaceable components. The same program can combine high-level abstractions with low-level memory access where performance or platform integration requires it.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: RAII → constructors/destructors → move semantics → smart pointers → STL containers → exceptions → concurrency.

topics.title: Environment Setup
topics.description: Learn the C++ development workflow, compilers, source files, linking, build tools, and how to work with diagnostics.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A C++ program passes through a toolchain rather than running directly from the source file. The compiler parses the source, checks types and language rules, and generates machine-oriented output. Multiple translation units can then be combined by the linker. Headers commonly provide declarations needed while compiling a source file, while definitions are compiled into one or more translation units.

When learning, keep the workflow deliberately small: create one `.cpp` file, compile it, read the first useful diagnostic, correct the program, and run it. Compiler messages are part of the learning process. A warning can indicate a conversion, unused value, or other suspicious behavior even when the program technically compiles.

As projects grow, a build system such as CMake can record source files, compiler options, libraries, and build targets. The important concept is that a successful build is a repeatable process rather than a collection of commands remembered by hand.

The important part of setup is understanding what happens between editing a `.cpp` file and seeing output. The preprocessor handles directives such as includes, the compiler translates each translation unit and checks language rules, and the linker resolves references between compiled units and libraries. A failure at each stage has a different character: preprocessing problems involve directives and included content, compiler problems involve source-language rules and types, and linker problems often involve missing or mismatched definitions.

For learning, compile small programs frequently. Use a modern language standard such as C++17 or newer when your project allows it, and enable useful warnings. Warnings often expose suspicious conversions, unreachable logic, or other mistakes before they become runtime bugs. A repeatable build command also matters because it makes experiments reproducible instead of depending on IDE-specific settings.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Practice compiling one file, then two files, and deliberately introduce a compiler error so you learn to read diagnostics.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Distinguish preprocessing, compilation, and linking. Know that a project can contain multiple translation units and that declarations in headers must match definitions supplied by source files or libraries. Be prepared to diagnose the difference between a compiler error and a linker error.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Assuming an IDE is the compiler, compiling only one source file from a multi-file project, ignoring warnings, or mixing incompatible language standards and library binaries. Another frequent mistake is believing that a successful compile guarantees correct runtime behavior.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Treat the build as a reproducible pipeline: source text is preprocessed, each translation unit is compiled, object files are linked, and the resulting program is loaded and executed. When something fails, identify the stage first; this sharply narrows the possible cause.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: You need to understand why a source file can compile successfully yet fail during linking, or why compiler flags affect both correctness and diagnostics.
Avoid: Treating the compiler as a single black box; preprocessing, compilation, assembly, and linking solve different problems.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A CI build commonly enables warnings, a chosen language standard, optimization, sanitizers in test jobs, and reproducible dependency versions. A missing symbol at link time is investigated differently from a syntax error.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: preprocessing → translation units → object files → linker → libraries → build systems such as CMake.

topics.title: Basic Syntax
topics.description: Learn declarations, statements, expressions, blocks, identifiers, includes, main(), and the syntax conventions used throughout C++.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
C++ syntax describes how declarations, expressions, statements, functions, and blocks are assembled into a valid program. Braces establish blocks, semicolons terminate many statements, and identifiers are case-sensitive. The compiler uses this structure to determine what each piece of source code means.

It is useful to distinguish syntax from semantics. A syntactically valid expression can still perform the wrong operation. For example, an arithmetic expression may compile but use integer division when a fractional result was intended. Learning C++ therefore requires asking not only “does this compile?” but also “what does this expression actually evaluate to?”

Formatting is not merely cosmetic. Consistent indentation makes ownership, nesting, conditions, and lifetime boundaries visible. This becomes especially valuable when reading templates, exception paths, or deeply nested control flow.

C++ syntax is easier to learn when you see a program as a hierarchy. A translation unit contains declarations and definitions; functions contain statements; statements contain expressions; and blocks group related statements. Braces therefore do more than improve formatting: they define the structure of control flow and can introduce a narrower scope.

Declarations tell the compiler what an entity is, while definitions provide the entity itself where required. For example, a function can be declared before `main` and defined later. Expressions produce values or perform operations, while statements use those expressions to control program behavior. Once these roles are clear, compiler diagnostics become easier to interpret because you can ask whether the problem is a missing declaration, invalid expression, malformed statement, or incorrect block structure.

Use consistent indentation, meaningful names, and small functions from the beginning. These habits make syntax errors and logical mistakes much easier to locate.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use clean syntax and formatting as the base for every later C++ topic.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain declarations, definitions, expressions, statements, scopes, and blocks. Be able to distinguish a syntax error from a semantically incorrect but valid program, and explain why operator precedence or implicit conversion can change behavior.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Missing semicolons, mismatched braces, using an identifier before declaration, confusing assignment with comparison, and assuming that code which compiles must be logically correct. Overusing clever one-line expressions also hurts readability.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: C++ source is hierarchical. Translation units contain declarations and definitions; functions contain statements; statements contain expressions; and braces establish nested scopes. Understanding that hierarchy makes compiler diagnostics much easier to interpret.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Building small programs or reading unfamiliar C++ quickly; focus on declarations, expressions, statements, scopes, and types before advanced abstractions.
Avoid: Assuming syntax alone explains behavior—initialization, lifetime, overload resolution, and conversions often determine what the code actually does.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: Clear braces, narrow scopes, explicit types where they aid readability, and consistent initialization make code easier to review and less error-prone.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: expressions → types → scope → initialization → functions → classes.

topics.title: Comments in C++
topics.description: Learn how to write useful comments that explain intent, constraints, invariants, and non-obvious design decisions.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Comments are part of the communication layer of a C++ program. The compiler does not execute them, so their value comes from helping another developer understand intent, constraints, invariants, or non-obvious decisions.

The most useful comments explain why the code has a particular shape. A comment such as “increment i” adds little because the statement already shows that. A comment explaining that an index is intentionally retained because it corresponds to an external record is much more valuable.

Comments should not become a second, outdated version of the program. If implementation changes, a comment that describes old behavior can actively mislead the reader. Prefer clear names and simple code first, then use comments for the reasoning that cannot be inferred easily from the code itself.

Comments are most useful when they preserve knowledge that the code alone cannot easily communicate. Examples include why a limit exists, why an unusual algorithm was selected, what external constraint a function assumes, or what invariant must remain true. Comments should not replace clear naming or structure; if the code is difficult to understand because a function is enormous, adding many comments is usually less effective than splitting the function.

Comments can also become dangerous when they describe behavior that is no longer true. Treat important comments as part of the maintenance responsibility of the code. When an assumption changes, update the comment at the same time.

For public APIs, documentation comments can describe parameters, return values, ownership expectations, exceptions, and constraints. For internal code, short comments should usually explain intent. A reader should be able to understand what the program does from the code and use comments to understand why a non-obvious choice was made.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Document invariants and non-obvious design decisions in production code.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain why comments should document intent, invariants, constraints, and non-obvious decisions rather than restating syntax. For public interfaces, mention documentation of ownership, preconditions, postconditions, and failure behavior.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Writing comments that become stale, explaining obvious code, using comments to justify unnecessarily complicated logic, or documenting behavior that the implementation no longer follows. If a comment is required to explain a huge function, first consider simplifying the function.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A comment is maintenance information that the compiler cannot enforce. Code should express what happens; comments are most valuable for explaining why it must happen that way or what external constraint caused the design.

topics.title: Data Types
topics.description: Understand built-in types, enumerations, aliases, numeric representation, and how type choice affects program behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A type determines what values an object can represent and which operations are valid for those values. Built-in types such as integers, floating-point values, `bool`, and character types provide the foundation, while classes, structures, enumerations, arrays, and templates allow richer models.

Do not assume that every numeric type has the same size on every platform. When exact representation matters, choose an appropriate fixed-width type such as `std::int32_t`, and when storage size itself matters, inspect it with `sizeof`. Type selection should reflect meaning and range rather than habit.

Enumerations are particularly useful when a variable represents a finite set of states. `enum class` keeps enumerator names scoped and reduces accidental conversions, making state-heavy programs easier to reason about.

A type is not merely a label; it determines what values an object can represent, which operations are meaningful, and how expressions involving that object are interpreted. Choosing a type is therefore part of program design. An integer is appropriate for counts, a Boolean for a true/false state, and a floating-point type for measurements where approximate numeric representation is acceptable.

C++ also distinguishes signed and unsigned integer types, and their ranges depend on the implementation and type width. When an exact representation size matters, fixed-width types from `<cstdint>` can make the requirement explicit. Character handling also deserves care because `char` represents a character-sized object but its signedness is implementation-dependent, while wider character facilities have their own semantics.

User-defined types such as `enum class`, `struct`, and `class` allow the program to express domain concepts directly. Stronger types can prevent invalid combinations and make interfaces easier to understand, which is often more valuable than choosing a type merely because it is convenient.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Choose types based on meaning, range, precision, and portability requirements.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Discuss built-in types, user-defined types, signed versus unsigned integers, `enum class`, and fixed-width integers. Mention that exact sizes are implementation-dependent unless a suitable fixed-width type is selected.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Assuming `int` is always 32 bits, using floating point for exact monetary arithmetic without considering domain requirements, mixing signed and unsigned values casually, and treating `enum class` like an implicitly convertible integer.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A type is a contract about representable values and valid operations. Choosing a type is therefore a design decision: the type should match the domain meaning, required range, precision, portability, and interface expectations.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Choosing representations based on range, precision, ownership, and interoperability requirements.
Avoid: Picking `int` or `double` by habit when the domain has stronger requirements.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A protocol field may need a fixed-width unsigned type, a monetary quantity may need a deliberate representation, and a count may use a suitable unsigned or signed type depending on the API contract.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: conversions → overflow → alignment → `std::int32_t`/fixed-width types → enums → templates.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Recording intent, invariants, non-obvious constraints, or why an unusual implementation is necessary.
Avoid: Comments that merely repeat the code or become stale specifications.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A useful comment explains why a lock is acquired before a callback, why a timeout exists, or which external protocol rule a seemingly strange conversion follows.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: naming → API documentation → invariants → code review → maintainability.

topics.title: Variable Types
topics.description: Learn variables, initialization, assignment, type deduction, value categories, and the foundations of object state.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A variable gives a name to an object with a particular type and lifetime. Initialization establishes its starting state; assignment changes the value of an already-existing object. These are different operations and should not be mentally merged.

Modern C++ offers several initialization forms. Brace initialization is often a good default because it makes narrowing conversions harder to introduce silently. Type deduction with `auto` can reduce repetition when the initializer already makes the intended type obvious, but it should not be used when hiding the type would make the code harder to understand.

C++ also distinguishes expressions by value category. An lvalue generally identifies an existing object, while an rvalue is commonly a temporary result. This distinction becomes important with references, move semantics, and overload resolution. Understanding it gradually is more useful than memorizing isolated definitions.

Initialization and assignment should be treated as different operations. Initialization creates an object with its initial state, while assignment changes an already existing object. This distinction becomes especially important for classes because construction can acquire resources or establish invariants that ordinary assignment does not reproduce.

Brace initialization is a useful default because it makes many narrowing conversions ill-formed instead of silently accepting them. For example, placing a fractional value into an integer with braces requires the programmer to confront the conversion. This reduces accidental data loss.

The lvalue/rvalue distinction becomes more important as C++ grows more advanced. An lvalue generally denotes an identifiable object, while an rvalue commonly represents a temporary result. References can bind to lvalues, and rvalue references enable move operations that transfer resources from temporary objects. You do not need to master move semantics immediately, but understanding that objects have identity, values have types, and temporaries have lifetimes prepares you for efficient modern C++.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Initialize objects deliberately and use `auto` when it improves readability rather than hiding an important type.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain initialization versus assignment, `auto`, brace initialization, and the basics of lvalues and rvalues. Be ready to explain why `auto` preserves the initializer's deduced type rather than simply meaning 'any type'.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Leaving variables uninitialized, using `auto` where the actual type is important to the reader, introducing narrowing conversions, and confusing an object's lifetime with the lifetime of a value stored in it.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: An object has a type, identity, storage duration, and lifetime. Initialization establishes its initial state; later assignment changes that state. Modern C++ design becomes safer when those distinctions remain explicit.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Modeling state whose type and lifetime should be obvious from the declaration.
Avoid: Overusing `auto` when the deduced type is important to understanding an API, or using implicit narrowing conversions.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: `auto` is especially useful for iterator and factory return types, while explicit types can be clearer at domain boundaries such as IDs and quantities.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: initialization → type deduction → lvalues/rvalues → const correctness → lifetime.

topics.title: Variable Scope
topics.description: Understand scope, lifetime, shadowing, and how limiting visibility makes programs easier to reason about.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Scope answers where a name can be used; lifetime answers how long the associated object exists. These concepts are related but not identical. A name can go out of scope while an object remains alive through another owner, and an object can have a lifetime that begins and ends inside a very small scope.

Keeping variables in the narrowest useful scope reduces accidental dependencies. If a value is needed only inside one loop, declaring it outside the entire function makes its possible uses larger than necessary. Small scopes also make resource lifetime easier to visualize.

Be careful with shadowing, where an inner declaration uses the same name as an outer declaration. It is legal C++, but excessive shadowing can make it difficult to determine which object an expression refers to.

Scope answers where a name is visible; lifetime answers how long the associated object exists. These ideas are related but not identical. A local variable can be visible only inside a block and exist for that block's execution, while a static object can have a much longer lifetime even though access to its name may be limited.

Narrow scope is usually easier to reason about because fewer parts of the program can interact with a variable. If a variable is only needed inside one loop, declare it there. If state is shared across several functions, consider whether it should instead be represented by an object passed through an explicit interface.

Shadowing is legal, but repeated reuse of the same name in nested scopes can make debugging difficult because the reader must constantly determine which object is being referenced. Good scope design reduces accidental coupling and makes ownership and lifetime easier to see. In larger programs, namespaces and class scope further organize names without requiring everything to be global.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Keep variables close to their use and avoid unnecessary shared scope.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Distinguish scope from lifetime and linkage. Explain block scope, namespace scope, and shadowing, and be prepared to discuss why narrow scope reduces accidental coupling.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Creating unnecessary globals, shadowing important variables, returning references to local objects, and assuming that leaving a scope is merely about name visibility rather than object lifetime and destruction.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Scope controls where a name can be written; lifetime controls when the associated object exists. Keeping names close to their use makes both dependencies and lifetimes easier to reason about.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Limiting where state can be accessed and reducing accidental coupling.
Avoid: Global mutable state when a narrower lifetime or explicit dependency would work.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: Keeping a temporary inside the smallest possible block prevents later code from depending accidentally on stale state.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: lifetime → linkage → namespaces → static storage duration → dependency injection.

topics.title: Constants And Literals
topics.description: Learn literals, constants, const correctness, constexpr, and how named values improve readability and safety.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Literals are values written directly in source code, while named constants give those values meaning. A number such as `18` may be correct but ambiguous; a constant such as `MaximumRetries` communicates why that number exists.

`const` expresses that an object should not be modified through that object. `constexpr` goes further by allowing an expression to participate in compile-time evaluation when the initializer satisfies the rules. Compile-time constants can improve readability and can be required in contexts where a constant expression is needed.

Pay attention to literal types. An integer literal, floating-point literal, character literal, and string literal have different types and semantics. Suffixes can also influence the type of a literal, which matters when overload resolution or numeric conversions are involved.

Literals are raw values written directly in source code, while named constants give those values meaning. The difference matters because `500` alone tells the reader very little, whereas `MaxConnections` communicates intent. Named constants also provide a single place to change a policy value.

`const` expresses that an object should not be modified through that object, while `constexpr` communicates that a value can participate in constant-expression evaluation when its initializer satisfies the language rules. `const` is therefore primarily about immutability through an interface, whereas `constexpr` also concerns compile-time evaluation.

Literal suffixes can influence type, especially for large integers and floating-point values. Hexadecimal and other bases are useful for bit masks and low-level values. String literals are arrays of characters with special language rules, and character literals represent individual characters. Learning to recognize the type of a literal helps prevent surprising conversions when expressions combine values of different types.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Replace unexplained numeric literals with meaningful named constants.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Compare literals, `const`, and `constexpr`. Explain that `constexpr` supports constant-expression evaluation when the expression satisfies the language rules, while `const` primarily expresses non-modification through a particular access path.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Assuming every `const` value is a compile-time constant, hiding important units in unnamed numbers, and overlooking literal types or suffixes when overload resolution and conversions matter.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Replace unexplained literals with named values that encode meaning. Then use `const` or `constexpr` according to whether the requirement is immutability, compile-time evaluation, or both.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Giving policy values and protocol constants meaningful names and, where appropriate, compile-time guarantees.
Avoid: Magic numbers scattered through business logic.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: Retry limits, buffer sizes, protocol versions, and conversion factors can be named constants so their meaning is visible during review.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: `const` → `constexpr` → constant expressions → enum class → literal types.

topics.title: Modifier Types
topics.description: Understand qualifiers and modifiers including const, volatile, mutable, and qualified pointer declarations.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Type qualifiers and related modifiers change how objects can be accessed or how declarations behave. `const` is the most common example: it communicates that an object should not be changed through a particular access path.

Pointer declarations deserve careful reading. `const int*` means the pointed-to integer is treated as const through that pointer, while `int* const` means the pointer itself cannot be reseated. Both can be combined when neither the pointer nor the pointed-to value should be modified through that declaration.

`volatile` has a specialized low-level purpose for objects whose values may change outside ordinary compiler-visible execution, such as certain hardware interfaces. It does not make ordinary multithreaded access safe. For threads, synchronization primitives and atomic operations are the relevant tools.

Type qualifiers become easier to understand when you ask what is being restricted: the object, the pointer, or the way the program observes a value. `const int` means the integer cannot be modified through that const object. `const int*` means the pointed-to integer cannot be modified through that pointer, while `int* const` means the pointer itself cannot be reseated.

`volatile` has a specialized purpose. It tells the implementation that accesses to an object are significant and may change outside ordinary optimization assumptions. This can matter for certain hardware or memory-mapped interfaces, but it does not make compound operations atomic and does not replace mutexes or atomics for thread synchronization.

`mutable` is mainly useful for class members that represent internal state such as a cache or bookkeeping value. The key lesson is to read qualifiers precisely and decide whether the protected entity is data, an address, or an observation mechanism. Clear declarations make interfaces safer because the compiler can enforce intended restrictions.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use qualifiers to communicate which part of an object or pointer may be modified.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Read declarations such as `const int*`, `int* const`, and `const int* const` correctly. Explain that `volatile` is not a threading primitive and that `mutable` has a narrow role in class design.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Saying `volatile` makes data thread-safe, confusing a const pointer with a pointer to const data, and adding qualifiers without understanding which object or access path they constrain.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: When reading a qualified declaration, ask exactly what is qualified: the object, the pointer itself, or the access semantics. Precise reading prevents many pointer and concurrency mistakes.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Expressing constness, low-level observation requirements, or member-level mutability precisely.
Avoid: Using `volatile` as a substitute for atomic operations or thread synchronization.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A memory-mapped hardware register may require `volatile`, while a shared counter between threads needs an atomic or lock.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: const correctness → pointers → atomics → memory-mapped I/O → `mutable`.

topics.title: Storage Classes
topics.description: Understand storage duration, linkage, static, extern, and the modern role of auto and other storage-related concepts.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Storage-related concepts in C++ are easier to understand through lifetime and linkage than by memorizing old keyword definitions. `static` can mean different things depending on where it appears: it can give namespace-scope entities internal linkage or preserve the state of a local variable between calls.

`extern` is commonly used when a declaration refers to a definition provided elsewhere. In modern projects, namespaces and well-designed headers/source files usually provide a clearer organization than a large collection of global variables.

The modern meaning of `auto` is primarily type deduction. For example, `auto count = 12;` asks the compiler to deduce the type from the initializer. `register` is obsolete as a practical optimization request; modern compilers make optimization decisions themselves.

Modern C++ makes some older storage-class terminology less central, so it is more useful to focus on the underlying ideas: storage duration, linkage, and visibility. Storage duration describes how long an object exists. Linkage describes whether a name can refer to the same entity across translation units. Scope describes where the name can be used in source code.

A function-local `static` object has static storage duration and retains its value between calls. Namespace-scope `static` can restrict linkage, while `extern` can declare an entity whose definition is provided elsewhere. The modern `auto` keyword is primarily used for type deduction, allowing the compiler to determine the variable's type from its initializer.

Avoid using global state merely because it is easy to access. Shared mutable state creates hidden dependencies and makes testing harder. Prefer objects with clear ownership and explicit interfaces. Understanding storage duration is particularly important when references or pointers outlive the objects they refer to.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use static local state sparingly and prefer explicit objects when state is part of application design.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Discuss storage duration, linkage, `static`, `extern`, and modern `auto`. Explain that `static` has different effects depending on context and that `register` is obsolete as a practical optimization request.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Treating `static` as having one universal meaning, using global mutable state as a shortcut, or assuming `extern` creates a definition. Also avoid using storage-class terminology without distinguishing scope, linkage, and lifetime.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Think in three dimensions: scope tells where a name is visible, linkage tells whether names can refer to the same entity across translation units, and storage duration tells how long the object exists.

topics.shortDescription: Understand storage duration, linkage, static, extern, and the modern role of auto and other storage-related concepts.

modules.title: Operators and Control Flow
modules.description: Learn operators and control flow through explanations, examples, and practical exercises.

topics.title: Operators
topics.description: Master arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise, assignment, conditional, member-access, and pointer operators.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Operators are the vocabulary used to form expressions. Arithmetic operators transform numbers, relational operators compare values, logical operators combine conditions, bitwise operators manipulate individual bits, and member-access operators navigate objects.

Precedence controls how an expression is grouped, but relying heavily on precedence makes code harder to review. Parentheses are inexpensive and often make intent explicit. Short-circuit evaluation is also important: `A && B` does not need to evaluate `B` when `A` is false, while `A || B` can skip `B` when `A` is true.

Numeric conversions deserve special attention. Integer division discards the fractional part, while mixing signed and unsigned values can produce surprising comparisons or conversions. Make the intended type visible rather than hoping implicit conversions do exactly what you expect.

Operators are expressions with defined type and evaluation rules, so understanding them requires more than memorizing symbols. Arithmetic operators produce numeric results, relational operators produce Boolean results, logical operators combine conditions, and bitwise operators manipulate individual bits. Member-access operators such as `.` and `->` connect expressions to object members, while `::` selects names from a namespace or class scope.

Conversions happen during expressions, and this is where many subtle bugs begin. Integer division discards the fractional part, signed and unsigned operands can interact in surprising ways, and a smaller destination type can lose information. Parentheses are often a better communication tool than relying on precedence tables.

Short-circuit evaluation is also important. In `a && b`, `b` is evaluated only when necessary, and in `a || b`, `b` is skipped when `a` is already true. This can both improve efficiency and protect expressions that require a prior condition. Read complex expressions from left to right and make the intended evaluation order obvious.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use parentheses and explicit conversions when they make numeric or Boolean intent clearer.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain precedence, associativity, short-circuit evaluation, arithmetic conversions, and overloaded operators. Be ready to discuss why signed/unsigned mixing and integer division can produce surprising results.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Relying on remembered precedence instead of parentheses, expecting both sides of `&&` or `||` to execute, comparing incompatible numeric types casually, and writing operator overloads with surprising semantics.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: An operator is part of an expression with defined type and evaluation rules. Read the expression in terms of operands, conversions, grouping, and possible side effects rather than treating symbols as isolated punctuation.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Writing compact expressions whose precedence and conversion rules are understood by the reader.
Avoid: Dense expressions that depend on subtle precedence, overloaded operators with surprising semantics, or assumptions about evaluation order.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A validation expression can safely use short-circuiting to check a pointer before dereferencing it. Complex business logic is often clearer when split into named conditions.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: value categories → implicit conversions → precedence → short-circuiting → operator overloading.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Reasoning about storage duration and linkage, especially `static`, `extern`, and namespace-scope declarations.
Avoid: Treating “static” as one single behavior; its effect depends on where it appears.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: Internal linkage can keep implementation details private to a translation unit, while static local state persists across calls but introduces shared state and synchronization concerns.

topics.title: Loop Types
topics.description: Learn while, do-while, for, range-based for, nested loops, break, continue, and how to reason about termination.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Loops repeatedly execute a block while some condition or iteration policy remains true. The key skill is not memorizing `for` versus `while`; it is identifying the state that changes and proving that the loop will eventually stop when it should.

A `for` loop is natural when initialization, condition, and update form one clear iteration pattern. `while` works well when the update or stopping condition is more event-driven. `do-while` is useful when the body must execute before the first condition check. Range-based `for` is often the clearest choice when traversing a standard container.

Nested loops multiply work. A loop over `n` elements inside another loop over `n` elements can require roughly `n²` iterations. That may be perfectly appropriate for a small grid but problematic for a large dataset, so correctness and performance should both be considered.

A loop should be understood as a state transition rather than simply a repeated block. At each iteration, the program has some state, evaluates a condition or obtains the next element, performs work, and updates state so that the loop can eventually terminate. If the update does not move the state toward the termination condition, an unintended infinite loop can result.

`while` is natural when repetition depends primarily on a condition, `for` is convenient when initialization, condition, and update form one compact iteration pattern, and `do-while` is appropriate when the body must execute before the condition is checked. Range-based `for` is usually the clearest choice when traversing a standard collection.

Nested loops require additional reasoning because their work multiplies. A loop over 1,000 records containing another loop over 1,000 records may perform roughly one million inner iterations. `break` and `continue` are useful control tools, but they should make the loop easier to understand rather than hide complicated flow.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use the loop form that makes initialization, termination, and progress easiest to verify.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Compare `for`, `while`, `do-while`, and range-based `for`. Explain termination, loop invariants, nested-loop complexity, and the role of `break` and `continue`.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Off-by-one errors, modifying an iterator or index incorrectly, accidentally creating infinite loops, and using nested loops where a standard algorithm or better data structure would reduce complexity.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Every loop should have a clear state, a condition, and progress toward termination. For a loop over a collection, range-based iteration often expresses intent more directly than manual index management.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Repeating work over a known range, condition, or stream of input.
Avoid: Loops whose termination condition is difficult to prove or whose body silently changes the collection being traversed.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: Range-based `for` is usually the clearest way to process container elements; indexed loops remain useful when an index is part of the logic.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: iterators → ranges → loop invariants → complexity → iterator invalidation.

topics.title: Decision-Making Statements
topics.description: Learn if, else, switch, conditional expressions, validation, branching, and clear decision-making design.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Decision statements choose a path based on a condition. An `if` statement is appropriate for general Boolean logic, while `switch` is useful when one expression is matched against discrete cases.

A good conditional structure validates assumptions at the boundary of the program and then allows the main logic to operate on trusted state. This reduces repeated checks and makes the normal path easier to read.

With `switch`, remember that cases can fall through unless control is stopped or intentional fall-through syntax is used. The conditional operator is useful for short value selection, but once it contains nested or complicated expressions, a normal `if` statement is usually clearer.

Decision-making is fundamentally about partitioning possible program states. A condition should answer a clear question, such as whether an amount is valid, whether a record exists, or whether a retry limit has been reached. When several conditions are combined, write them so their business meaning is visible rather than constructing a dense Boolean expression that requires mental decoding.

`if` is flexible for ranges and unrelated conditions. `switch` is useful when one expression is compared against discrete cases. Remember that ordinary `switch` cases can fall through unless control is stopped, commonly with `break` or an explicit return. The conditional operator is useful for a small value selection but becomes harder to read when nested.

Validation should happen before unsafe operations. For example, check that an index is within the valid range before indexing, and verify input state before converting or using it. Good decisions are not only about choosing the correct branch; they also make invalid states difficult to reach.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Build validation and state-dependent behavior with clear branches and exhaustive cases.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Compare `if`, `switch`, and the conditional operator. Explain fall-through in `switch`, validation at boundaries, and how to keep complex business conditions readable.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Forgetting a `break` where fall-through was not intended, writing deeply nested conditionals, using `==` where assignment was intended, and failing to handle an unexpected/default state.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A conditional partitions possible program states. Good branching makes those partitions explicit and handles invalid or unexpected states close to the boundary where they are detected.

modules.title: Functions
modules.description: Learn functions through explanations, examples, and practical exercises.

topics.title: Functions
topics.description: Understand function declarations, definitions, parameters, return values, references, pointers, overloads, defaults, and decomposition.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A function gives a name and boundary to a unit of behavior. A useful function has a clear input contract, a predictable result or side effect, and a responsibility that can be understood without reading the entire program.

Passing by value gives the function its own parameter object. Passing by reference lets the function work directly with an existing object, while `const` references are commonly used to avoid copying a larger object without allowing modification. Pointers are useful when address semantics or an optional target are meaningful.

Overloading lets several functions share a name when their parameter lists distinguish them. Keep overload sets coherent: callers should be able to predict which operation a particular call represents. Default arguments can simplify APIs, but excessive defaults can make behavior less obvious.

A function is a contract between its caller and implementation. The declaration communicates the function's name, parameters, and return type, while the definition supplies the behavior. A good function has a focused responsibility and a clear relationship between its inputs, outputs, side effects, and failure behavior.

Passing by value is appropriate when a copy is cheap or when the function should work with its own value. A reference allows direct access to an existing object, while a const reference can avoid copying a larger object without allowing modification. Pointers are useful when nullability or explicit address semantics are meaningful. These choices communicate intent to both the compiler and the reader.

Function decomposition also improves debugging. If a program has separate functions for parsing, validation, calculation, and output, a defect can be isolated to a smaller region. Overloading should be used when several operations are genuinely the same conceptual operation with different parameter types. Avoid creating overload sets that force readers to guess which behavior a call represents.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Break larger programs into small functions with focused responsibilities and clear contracts.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain declarations versus definitions, pass-by-value, references, pointers, `const` parameters, overloading, default arguments, and return-value design. Be ready to connect function signatures with ownership and mutability.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Returning references or pointers to local objects, copying large objects unnecessarily, creating ambiguous overloads, hiding side effects, and using default arguments as a substitute for a clear API.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A function is a contract. Its signature should communicate what it needs, what it can modify, what it returns, and whether absence or ownership transfer is possible.

modules.description: Learn functions and numeric programming through explanations, examples, and practical exercises.

topics.title: Numbers
topics.description: Learn integer and floating-point arithmetic, math facilities, random generation, precision, overflow, and numeric comparisons.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Numeric programming requires understanding both representation and operations. Integer arithmetic is exact only within the representable range, while floating-point values approximate real numbers and can accumulate rounding error.

For floating-point comparisons, exact equality is often inappropriate. A tolerance-based comparison is usually better when the values come from calculations. The correct tolerance depends on the scale and meaning of the values, so there is no universal epsilon that works for every problem.

For random values, modern C++ provides engines and distributions through `<random>`. Separating the random engine from the distribution makes the desired range and statistical behavior explicit. Numeric code should also consider overflow, signed/unsigned conversions, and the required precision.

Numeric programming requires attention to representation, range, and precision. Integers represent whole values exactly within their supported range, but signed overflow has language-level consequences that should not be treated like ordinary wraparound. Unsigned types have modular arithmetic behavior, yet mixing signed and unsigned values can produce unexpected comparisons or conversions.

Floating-point values are approximations. A decimal such as 0.1 generally cannot be represented exactly in binary floating-point, so calculations can accumulate small differences. For this reason, comparing two floating-point results with `==` is often inappropriate when the values come from independent calculations. A tolerance-based comparison is usually better, with the tolerance chosen for the scale and requirements of the problem.

For random values, modern `<random>` facilities separate the random engine from the distribution. This makes the intended range and distribution explicit. For mathematical operations, `<cmath>` provides reusable functions. Always choose a numeric type according to the domain requirement rather than defaulting automatically to `int` or `double`.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use appropriate numeric types and tolerant comparisons when calculations involve floating-point values.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain integer overflow, signed/unsigned conversions, floating-point approximation, tolerance-based comparison, and the separation of random engines from distributions in `<random>`.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Using `==` for independently computed floating-point values, assuming signed overflow wraps predictably, using integer division accidentally, and treating `double` as an exact decimal type.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Numeric correctness depends on representation as much as arithmetic. Before choosing an operation, determine the required range, precision, rounding behavior, and failure mode.

topics.title: Arrays
topics.description: Understand built-in arrays, indexing, bounds, contiguous storage, std::array, std::vector, and array traversal.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
An array stores a fixed number of elements of one type in contiguous memory. Its indexing begins at zero, so an array containing `N` elements has valid indexes from `0` through `N - 1`.

The most important array rule is bounds safety. C++ does not automatically stop an out-of-range built-in array access. Reading or writing outside the object is undefined behavior and can corrupt unrelated data or cause unpredictable failures.

For modern C++, `std::array` is often preferable when the size is fixed and should be part of the type, while `std::vector` is a better fit for a dynamically sized sequence. These containers integrate naturally with standard algorithms and provide clearer interfaces than manually managed arrays.

An array's most important property is contiguous storage with a fixed number of elements. Indexing translates naturally into an offset from the first element, which is why array access is efficient. The same property also explains why an out-of-range index is dangerous: the language does not automatically turn an invalid index into a safe access to another element.

When an array is passed to a function, it commonly decays to a pointer to its first element, so the function usually needs a separate element count. This is why a parameter such as `const int values[]` does not by itself preserve the array's size. `std::array` keeps the size as part of the type, while `std::vector` manages a dynamically sized contiguous sequence.

Think of array operations as simple algorithms: traversal, search, aggregation, transformation, and update. For each algorithm, define the valid index range first. When using multidimensional arrays, decide what each dimension represents and keep the row/column interpretation consistent throughout the program.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Prefer `std::array` for fixed-size collections and `std::vector` for dynamically sized sequences.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Compare built-in arrays, `std::array`, and `std::vector`. Explain zero-based indexing, contiguous storage, array-to-pointer decay, and why out-of-bounds access is undefined behavior.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Using `N` as a valid index for an `N`-element array, losing the array size when passing it to a function, and manually managing dynamic arrays when a standard container would express the requirement more safely.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: An array is a contiguous sequence with a fixed extent. `std::array` preserves that extent in its type; `std::vector` owns a dynamically sized contiguous sequence. Choose the representation that matches the required lifetime and size semantics.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: You need fixed-size contiguous storage or are interfacing with APIs that expose raw arrays.
Avoid: Manual bounds assumptions; prefer `std::array` or `std::vector` when their ownership and size semantics fit.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: `std::array` works well for fixed protocol fields, while `std::vector` fits dynamically sized records and provides managed storage.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: contiguous storage → pointers → spans → vectors → iterator invalidation → bounds safety.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Arithmetic has explicit range, precision, rounding, and error requirements.
Avoid: Assuming floating-point values are exact or that signed overflow behaves like ordinary machine wraparound.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A financial or measurement system should define its numeric representation and rounding policy rather than relying on accidental floating-point behavior.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: integer promotions → floating point → `<cmath>` → `<random>` → numeric limits → overflow.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Giving behavior a focused contract with explicit inputs, outputs, side effects, and failure behavior.
Avoid: Functions that silently mutate unrelated global state or have many unrelated responsibilities.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: Separating parsing, validation, calculation, and persistence lets each function be tested and reasoned about independently.

sections.title: Related concepts

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid

Use it when: Translating mutually exclusive states, validation rules, or state-machine transitions into explicit branches.
Avoid: Deeply nested conditionals when a guard clause, function extraction, or polymorphic design would make the decision easier to verify.

sections.content: Production scenario: Validate request state before performing an expensive operation, and make the invalid paths explicit rather than letting them fall through.

topics.title: Strings
topics.description: Learn C-style strings, null termination, std::string, searching, slicing, modification, and input behavior.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
C++ supports both C-style null-terminated character sequences and the higher-level `std::string` abstraction. A C-style string depends on a terminating `\0`, so its buffer must always have room for the characters plus that terminator.

`std::string` manages its own storage and provides operations such as searching, slicing, appending, comparison, and size queries. This removes much of the manual capacity bookkeeping that makes C-style strings error-prone.

Input style also matters. `operator>>` reads formatted tokens and normally stops at whitespace, while `std::getline` reads an entire line. Mixing the two requires understanding the newline left in the input stream so that the next line read behaves as intended.

Strings are a common source of confusion because C++ supports both C-style null-terminated character sequences and the safer, richer `std::string` abstraction. A C-style string is not merely an array of characters; it must contain a terminating `\0` before functions that expect a null-terminated sequence can safely determine its length.

`std::string` manages its own storage and provides operations such as concatenation, searching, substring extraction, comparison, and size queries. This makes it the preferred representation for most ordinary text in modern C++. Input also needs deliberate handling: `operator>>` normally reads a token and stops at whitespace, while `std::getline` reads an entire line. Switching between the two requires attention to the newline remaining in the input stream.

Capacity is a correctness issue when using character buffers. Any operation that writes into a fixed buffer must account for the terminating null character and available space. For APIs, use `const std::string&` when a read-only reference is appropriate, or pass by value when taking ownership or intentionally making a copy is useful.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Prefer `std::string` for normal text handling and learn C-style strings mainly for interoperability and low-level work.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Compare `std::string` with C-style null-terminated character sequences. Explain `getline` versus formatted extraction and the importance of capacity and the terminating null character for C APIs.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Forgetting the `\0` terminator in manual buffers, mixing `>>` and `getline` without handling the remaining newline, assuming a string literal is a modifiable character array, and performing unchecked buffer writes.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Text has both representation and ownership. `std::string` manages its character storage and size, while C APIs often require a pointer to a null-terminated sequence. Conversions across that boundary require explicit lifetime and capacity reasoning.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: `std::string` is the normal representation for owned text and C-style strings are required only for interoperability.
Avoid: Passing arbitrary character buffers to APIs that require null termination without proving capacity and termination.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: Parse a request into `std::string`, validate its contents, and convert to a C-style representation only at an API boundary that explicitly requires it.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: `std::string_view` → encoding → `getline` → null termination → buffer capacity.

topics.title: Pointers
topics.description: Understand pointers, addresses, dereferencing, nullability, pointer arithmetic, pointer safety, and ownership boundaries.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A pointer is an object whose value represents an address or pointer value. The address-of operator obtains a pointer to an object, and dereferencing a valid pointer accesses the pointed-to object.

The difficult part of pointer programming is not the syntax; it is validity. Before dereferencing, the pointer must identify a suitable live object, the access must respect the type and permissions, and the object must remain alive for the duration of the access. A null pointer does not identify a usable object.

Pointer arithmetic has a defined relationship with array elements. It should not be treated as general integer arithmetic. In modern C++, raw pointers are often best used for non-owning access or low-level interfaces, while ownership is represented by RAII types such as `std::unique_ptr`.

Pointers become manageable when you separate three ideas: the pointer object, the address stored in it, and the lifetime of the object at that address. `int* p` creates a pointer object capable of storing the address of an `int`; `&value` obtains an address; and `*p` accesses the object at that address. These operations are simple individually, but correctness depends on whether the address is valid at the moment of dereference.

A pointer can be null, point to a valid object, point one past the end of an array for certain comparison/iteration purposes, or become dangling after the target's lifetime ends. Only some of these states permit dereferencing. Pointer arithmetic is meaningful within an array because the compiler knows the element type and therefore the step size.

Modern C++ uses raw pointers mainly for non-owning relationships or low-level interfaces. When a pointer represents ownership, smart pointers make that ownership explicit. `unique_ptr` communicates exclusive ownership, `shared_ptr` shared ownership, and `weak_ptr` non-owning observation of shared ownership. This reduces the number of manual lifetime decisions a program must get right.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use raw pointers primarily for non-owning or low-level access and make ownership explicit elsewhere.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain address-of, dereference, null pointers, dangling pointers, pointer arithmetic, and the distinction between ownership and non-owning access. Compare raw pointers with `unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`, and `weak_ptr` at a high level.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Dereferencing null or dangling pointers, deleting memory twice, returning pointers to local objects, performing pointer arithmetic outside an array relationship, and using `shared_ptr` simply because raw pointers feel difficult.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Always separate the pointer object, the address it contains, and the lifetime of the target object. A pointer is safe to dereference only when it points to an appropriate live object and the access is permitted.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Nullability, address semantics, non-owning access, or low-level interoperability are genuinely part of the contract.
Avoid: Using raw pointers as ambiguous ownership handles in application code.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A function can accept a pointer when “object may be absent” is meaningful, while ownership should normally be represented by `unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`, or a value type.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: lifetime → ownership → smart pointers → pointer arithmetic → dangling pointers → `std::span`.

topics.title: References
topics.description: Learn references, const references, reference parameters, lifetime rules, and how references differ from pointers.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A reference is an alias to an existing object rather than a separate nullable handle. An ordinary reference is initialized when it is created and is normally expected to remain associated with that object.

References are particularly useful for function parameters. A non-const reference communicates that the function may modify the caller's object. A `const` reference communicates that the function only observes the object and can often avoid a copy.

Pointers and references are not interchangeable. A pointer can represent “no object” with `nullptr` and can be changed to point elsewhere. A normal reference expresses that a valid object is required. Choosing between them is therefore part of designing a function's contract.

A reference is best viewed as an alias to an existing object rather than a small pointer with different syntax. An ordinary lvalue reference must bind to an object when it is initialized, and using the reference accesses the original object directly. This makes references convenient for function parameters when a function requires an existing object.

A const reference is especially useful for read-only access to larger objects because it avoids a copy while preventing modification through that reference. A non-const reference communicates that the function may modify the caller's object. These are interface decisions, not just syntax choices.

References have important lifetime rules. Returning a reference is safe only when the referred object will continue to exist after the function returns. Returning a reference to a local variable creates a dangling reference because the local object's lifetime ends when the function exits. Unlike ordinary pointers, references are not normally nullable or reseatable. When absence is meaningful, a pointer or another explicit optional representation may communicate the design better. Rvalue references add another dimension by enabling move operations for resource-owning objects.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use references when a function requires an existing object and pointers when nullability or explicit address semantics matter.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Compare references and pointers, explain const references, reference lifetime, rvalue references, and why a normal reference is not a nullable or reseatable handle.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Returning a reference to a local variable, storing a reference beyond the target's lifetime, assuming a reference can represent absence, and confusing `T&` with `const T&` semantics.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A reference expresses an aliasing relationship to an existing object. That stronger contract is useful when the callee requires a valid object; use a pointer or another explicit representation when absence is meaningful.
