topics.title: Date And Time
topics.description: Understand durations, time points, clocks, elapsed-time measurement, and the foundations of modern C++ time handling.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Time programming becomes clearer when three ideas are separated: a time point answers “when?”, a duration answers “how long?”, and a clock answers “according to which source of time?”.

For measuring elapsed execution time, `std::chrono::steady_clock` is usually appropriate because it is intended for monotonic interval measurement. A wall-clock time can change because of clock synchronization or calendar adjustments, so it is not the same thing as an elapsed-time measurement.

Calendar operations introduce additional concerns such as time zones, formatting, daylight-saving rules, and representation. Keep internal calculations in well-defined time units and convert to presentation formats only where needed.

Time APIs become easier when you distinguish a duration, a time point, and a clock. A duration answers how much time passed, a time point answers when an event occurred relative to a clock, and a clock supplies the time points. Mixing these concepts can produce confusing code, especially when converting between units.

For measuring elapsed time, `std::chrono::steady_clock` is generally appropriate because it is intended for monotonic interval measurement. A wall-clock time can change because of synchronization or system adjustments, so it is not always suitable for measuring how long an operation took.

Calendar dates introduce additional concerns such as time zones, daylight-saving changes, formatting, and parsing. Treat a timestamp as a specific point in time and convert it to a human-readable representation only at the appropriate boundary. For learning, first become comfortable with durations and elapsed-time measurement; then move to calendar operations. This prevents treating every date/time problem as if it were simply an integer count of seconds.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use `steady_clock` for elapsed-time measurements and keep duration calculations separate from calendar formatting.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Distinguish duration, time point, and clock. Explain why `steady_clock` is suitable for elapsed-time measurement and why wall-clock time is not a reliable stopwatch.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Measuring elapsed time with a wall clock that can be adjusted, mixing time units, ignoring time zones for calendar data, and assuming a timestamp automatically communicates the intended time zone.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Keep machine-level time calculations separate from human calendar presentation. Measure intervals with an appropriate clock, represent durations explicitly, and convert to local or formatted calendar forms only at the boundary.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Measuring elapsed time, representing time points, or converting between durations and calendar representations.
Avoid: Using wall-clock time to measure elapsed performance or mixing local calendar assumptions with absolute timestamps.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: Use a monotonic clock for request-duration metrics, while timestamps intended for users or distributed systems require an explicit time-zone/formatting policy.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: `std::chrono` → steady clocks → system clocks → durations → time zones → serialization.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: A valid existing object is required and aliasing that object communicates the function's contract clearly.
Avoid: Returning references to local objects or using references when absence/reseating is a meaningful state.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A read-only service function can accept `const Customer&` without copying the object; a mutating function can use `Customer&` when mutation is intentional.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: lvalue/rvalue references → move semantics → lifetime extension → reference collapsing → perfect forwarding.

topics.shortDescription: Understand durations, time points, clocks, elapsed-time measurement, and the foundations of modern C++ time handling.

topics.title: Basic Input/Output
topics.description: Learn standard streams, formatted input/output, line input, stream state, errors, and numeric formatting.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
C++ stream I/O uses objects such as `std::cin`, `std::cout`, `std::cerr`, and `std::clog` to communicate with standard input and output channels. The `>>` operator extracts formatted values, while `<<` inserts formatted output.

Input should be treated as fallible. If extraction fails because the user enters text where a number is expected, the stream enters a failure state. Robust programs detect that state, recover or reject the input, and avoid continuing with an invalid value.

Line-oriented input is useful when spaces belong to the data. Formatting manipulators such as `std::fixed` and `std::setprecision` control numeric presentation without changing the underlying stored value.

Streams provide a typed interface between the program and external input/output sources. `std::cin` extracts values from standard input, `std::cout` writes normal output, and `std::cerr` is commonly used for errors. The stream operators perform conversions according to the destination type, which is convenient but means the program must still check whether extraction succeeded.

A common input pattern is to initialize a variable, prompt the user, extract into it, and verify the stream state. If extraction fails, the variable should not be treated as though valid input was received. After a failed extraction, recovery may require clearing the error state and discarding invalid characters before trying again.

Formatted output is also part of the interface. `<iomanip>` can control precision, width, and formatting. Line-oriented input with `getline` should be chosen when spaces are meaningful. Mixing token extraction and line extraction is a common beginner issue because the newline left in the stream may be consumed immediately by the next `getline`. Understanding the stream as a sequence of characters makes this behavior predictable.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Validate input states and distinguish token input from line input.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain standard streams, formatted extraction, `getline`, stream state flags, and error recovery. Be prepared to explain why a failed extraction affects later reads.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Continuing after a failed numeric extraction, mixing token and line input without handling the pending newline, and assuming output formatting changes the underlying numeric value.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A stream represents a sequence plus state. Every read can succeed or fail, and the state determines what subsequent operations do. Robust input code treats external data as untrusted.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Reading formatted input or producing diagnostics and user-facing output with standard streams.
Avoid: Assuming input always succeeds or mixing formatted extraction and line input without handling stream state.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A command-line tool should validate stream state, report failures to `std::cerr`, and keep parsing logic separate from business logic.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: streams → formatting → `getline` → file streams → error states.

topics.shortDescription: Learn standard streams, formatted input/output, line input, stream state, errors, and numeric formatting.

topics.title: Data Structures
topics.description: Learn structures, member access, arrays of records, passing structures, aliases, and choosing struct versus class.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A structure groups related pieces of data into one user-defined type. This is useful whenever several values describe one conceptual entity, such as a measurement, product, or configuration record.

Member access uses `.` for an object and `->` for a pointer to an object. Structures can be passed by value, pointer, or reference. For read-only access to a larger structure, a `const` reference is often a good default because it avoids copying while documenting that the function will not modify the object.

C++ `struct` and `class` are both capable of containing data and functions. The important default difference is access: `struct` members are public by default, while `class` members are private by default. Choose the form that communicates whether the type is primarily an open data aggregate or an encapsulated abstraction.

A structure is useful when several pieces of data represent one logical entity. Instead of maintaining separate arrays such as `ids`, `names`, and `prices`, a record type can keep the related fields together. This improves readability because the relationship between values is represented directly in the type.

Passing a structure by value creates a copy, which is simple but may be more expensive for larger objects. Passing by const reference allows inspection without copying, while passing by non-const reference permits modification. A pointer can also be used when nullability or pointer semantics are required. For a pointer to a structure, `->` provides member access through the pointer.

`struct` and `class` are both capable of containing data and functions. Their most visible default difference is access: members of a struct are public by default, while members of a class are private by default. Choose based on design intent. Simple data aggregates often work well as structs, while classes are useful when operations and invariants should control how state changes.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Model related data as structures when an aggregate representation is clearer than separate variables.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Compare `struct` and `class`, explain member access through `.` and `->`, and discuss passing aggregates by value versus reference. Mention invariants when a structure becomes behavior-rich.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Using separate parallel arrays when a record type would preserve relationships, exposing mutable state that should be protected, and copying large aggregates unintentionally.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A data structure should represent a coherent concept. Start with an aggregate when data naturally travels together; introduce encapsulation when rules about that state need enforcement.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Choosing a representation based on access patterns, ownership, ordering, and complexity requirements.
Avoid: Choosing a data structure only because it is familiar.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A workload dominated by indexed access may favor a vector; frequent key lookup may favor a map or unordered map; queue-like processing calls for queue/deque semantics.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: STL containers → Big-O complexity → cache locality → iterators → ownership.

topics.shortDescription: Learn structures, member access, arrays of records, passing structures, aliases, and choosing struct versus class.

topics.title: Classes And Objects
topics.description: Understand classes, objects, constructors, destructors, access control, copying, this, static members, and object invariants.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
A class defines a type whose objects combine state and behavior. Constructors establish an initial valid state, member functions provide operations, and destructors participate in resource cleanup when an object's lifetime ends.

A class becomes useful when it can protect invariants. For example, if an account balance must follow certain rules, exposing the balance as public data allows every caller to bypass those rules. A controlled operation such as `deposit()` or `withdraw()` keeps the rule near the state it protects.

C++ object design also includes copying, moving, `this`, static members, and friendship. These features become easier to understand once you first establish a clear ownership and lifetime model for the object.

A class is a type definition that describes state and behavior; an object is a concrete instance with its own lifetime and state. The real value of a class is not simply grouping variables and methods. It is the ability to establish rules about valid state and expose operations that preserve those rules.

Constructors are responsible for establishing the initial state of an object. A well-designed constructor should leave the object usable according to the class invariant. Destructors run when an object's lifetime ends and are the foundation of RAII: resources can be tied to object lifetime so cleanup happens automatically.

Copy and move behavior becomes important when a class owns resources. The compiler can generate special member functions in many cases, but resource-owning classes must be designed carefully so copying does not accidentally duplicate ownership or create double release. Static members belong to the class rather than each object, while the `this` pointer identifies the current object in non-static member functions. Keep public interfaces small and protect state when unrestricted modification could violate invariants.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use classes to protect invariants and make valid operations explicit.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain class versus object, constructors, destructors, RAII, access control, `this`, static members, copy/move behavior, and invariants. Be ready to explain the Rule of Zero at a high level.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Writing a destructor unnecessarily, owning raw resources without a clear copy/move strategy, exposing all state publicly, and forgetting that constructor failure prevents a fully constructed object from existing.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A class should establish a valid state and control how that state changes. Resource-owning classes should tie resource lifetime to object lifetime so destruction is deterministic and exception-safe.

topics.shortDescription: Understand classes, objects, constructors, destructors, access control, copying, this, static members, and object invariants.

modules.title: Inheritance and Object Design
modules.description: Learn inheritance and object design through explanations, examples, and practical exercises.

topics.title: Inheritance
topics.description: Learn inheritance, base/derived relationships, public inheritance, multiple inheritance, composition, and substitutability.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Inheritance creates a relationship between a base type and a derived type. Public inheritance is most appropriate when a derived object genuinely satisfies the interface expectations of the base type.

The most important design question is whether substitution makes sense. If callers can use a derived object anywhere the base is expected without violating assumptions, inheritance may be appropriate. If the relationship is simply that one object contains or uses another, composition is usually clearer.

Multiple inheritance can be useful for combining independent interfaces, but it can also create ambiguity and diamond-shaped hierarchies. C++ provides virtual inheritance for some such cases, yet a simpler composition-based design is often preferable when polymorphic substitution is not required.

Inheritance is strongest when the derived type can genuinely be substituted for the base type. Public inheritance communicates an is-a relationship: code that expects the base abstraction should be able to use the derived object without violating the base contract. If that relationship does not hold, composition is often a better design.

A derived object contains a base-class subobject, and access to inherited members is controlled by access specifiers. Multiple inheritance can combine independent capabilities, but it can also introduce ambiguity when several inheritance paths contain the same base. Virtual inheritance can address particular diamond-shaped layouts, but it adds complexity and should not be used merely because the language supports it.

Inheritance also interacts with object lifetime and polymorphism. If a base class is used polymorphically, virtual functions allow calls through a base pointer or reference to reach the derived implementation. A polymorphic base normally needs a virtual destructor so deleting a derived object through a base pointer performs the correct destruction sequence. Prefer simple hierarchies and use composition when it expresses the relationship more naturally.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Choose inheritance for genuine substitutability; otherwise consider composition.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain public inheritance as an is-a/substitutability relationship and compare it with composition. Discuss multiple inheritance, virtual inheritance, and polymorphic base destructors.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Inheriting only to reuse code, slicing derived objects into base values, creating deep hierarchies, and deleting a derived object through a base pointer whose destructor is not virtual.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Inheritance is an interface and substitutability mechanism, not merely a code-reuse shortcut. If the derived type cannot satisfy the base contract, composition is usually the better abstraction.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: There is a genuine substitutability relationship and the base abstraction is designed for polymorphic use.
Avoid: Inheritance solely for code reuse when composition provides a clearer ownership and dependency model.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A `PaymentProcessor` interface can support multiple implementations when callers need substitutable behavior, while shared implementation details may be better composed from helper objects.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: virtual functions → slicing → virtual destructors → composition → Liskov substitution.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: An object has invariants, state, behavior, and resource/lifetime responsibilities that belong together.
Avoid: Creating classes that merely wrap fields without a useful contract or exposing mutable state unnecessarily.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A connection class can own a socket and guarantee cleanup in its destructor, making the valid state and lifetime explicit.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: constructors → destructors → RAII → copy/move → encapsulation → invariants.

topics.shortDescription: Learn inheritance, base/derived relationships, public inheritance, multiple inheritance, composition, and substitutability.

topics.title: Overloading: Operators And Functions
topics.description: Understand function overloading and operator overloading, overload resolution, intuitive operator semantics, and limitations.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Function overloading allows a family of operations to share one name when their parameter types or counts distinguish the calls. The compiler resolves an overload using the arguments and the language's conversion rules.

Operator overloading extends the same idea to user-defined types. A `Point` can reasonably support addition because adding two points can have an intuitive meaning. An operator should not be overloaded merely because the syntax is available; its behavior should match what readers naturally expect.

Operator precedence does not change when an operator is overloaded. The overloaded function still participates in the normal expression grammar, so parentheses may be needed when the intended grouping is not obvious.

Function overloading is compile-time selection among functions with the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler considers the arguments at the call site and chooses a viable overload. Overloads work best when the functions represent the same conceptual operation and differ only in the type or number of inputs.

Operator overloading extends this idea to user-defined types. A `Point` can define `operator+` so adding two points reads naturally, but the operator should preserve a meaning that users can reasonably predict. Operator precedence and the number of operands are determined by the language; an overload does not let you invent a new precedence rule.

Be careful with conversions because implicit conversions can make an overload set ambiguous or select an unexpected function. When an operation is complex or has surprising side effects, a named function is often clearer than an overloaded operator. Good operator design improves readability; clever operator design can make ordinary code difficult to understand.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Overload functions and operators only when the resulting interface is predictable.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain compile-time overload resolution, conversions, ambiguity, and sensible operator semantics. Be ready to explain why overloaded operators do not change language precedence.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Creating overloads that differ only in confusing conversions, giving operators surprising side effects, and assuming a user-defined operator can change the number of operands or precedence rules.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Overloading lets one conceptual operation accept different types or forms. The interface is successful when the reader can predict which overload is selected and what the operation means.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Multiple operations have the same conceptual meaning and can be distinguished naturally by parameter types.
Avoid: Overloading that makes conversions, ambiguity, or side effects surprising.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A value type such as `Money` can overload arithmetic and comparison operators when those operations preserve intuitive domain semantics.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: overload resolution → implicit conversions → templates → operator semantics → user-defined types.

topics.shortDescription: Understand function overloading and operator overloading, overload resolution, intuitive operator semantics, and limitations.

topics.title: Polymorphism
topics.description: Learn runtime and compile-time polymorphism, virtual functions, pure virtual functions, abstract classes, and virtual destructors.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Polymorphism means that one interface can represent multiple concrete implementations. In C++, runtime polymorphism is commonly implemented with virtual functions and base-class references or pointers.

A pure virtual function defines a required operation without providing a normal base implementation. A class containing such a function is abstract and is intended to describe a capability rather than be instantiated directly.

When a base class is used polymorphically, its destructor is commonly virtual so that destroying a derived object through a base pointer invokes the correct destructor chain. Compile-time polymorphism also exists through templates and overloads; the key difference is when the implementation choice is resolved.

Polymorphism separates the interface a caller depends on from the concrete implementation that performs the work. With runtime polymorphism, a base class exposes virtual operations and derived classes provide specialized behavior. A base reference or pointer can then refer to different derived objects while the caller uses the same interface.

A pure virtual function makes a class abstract, meaning the class represents a contract rather than a directly constructible concrete object. The derived class must implement the required operations before it can be instantiated. The `override` keyword is valuable because it asks the compiler to verify that a derived function really overrides a virtual base function.

Runtime polymorphism has a cost and a design trade-off: the call target is selected dynamically, and the program becomes dependent on a class hierarchy. Templates provide another form of polymorphism where behavior is selected during compilation. Choose runtime polymorphism when substitution and dynamic behavior are central; use templates or ordinary functions when the required behavior can be determined statically.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use runtime polymorphism when different implementations must satisfy one common contract.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Compare runtime polymorphism through virtual functions with compile-time polymorphism through templates and overloads. Explain pure virtual functions, `override`, abstract classes, and virtual destructors.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Forgetting `override`, omitting a virtual destructor in a polymorphic base, object slicing, and using runtime inheritance when static generic programming would be simpler.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Polymorphism separates a stable interface from multiple implementations. Runtime polymorphism chooses behavior through a base interface at execution time; templates choose behavior during compilation.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: One interface must support multiple implementations without exposing their concrete types.
Avoid: Runtime polymorphism when a value type, template, or variant would express the relationship more simply.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A service can depend on a payment interface while tests provide a deterministic implementation and production provides a real gateway implementation.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: virtual dispatch → abstract classes → object lifetime → templates → `std::variant`.

topics.shortDescription: Learn runtime and compile-time polymorphism, virtual functions, pure virtual functions, abstract classes, and virtual destructors.

topics.title: Data Abstraction
topics.description: Understand abstraction as stable interfaces that hide implementation details and reduce unnecessary coupling.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Abstraction focuses on exposing what a caller needs while hiding implementation details that the caller should not depend on. A good abstraction gives a stable interface while allowing the implementation behind that interface to change.

For example, a `CoffeeMachine::brew()` operation can hide the sequence of heating, grinding, and dispensing. A caller should not need to know the internal order unless that order is part of the public contract.

Abstraction is successful when it reduces unnecessary knowledge and coupling. Hiding every detail is not automatically good design; the interface still needs to expose enough meaningful operations for clients to use the type correctly.

Abstraction is about reducing the amount of implementation detail a user must understand. A good abstraction exposes operations that match the problem domain and hides steps that callers should not need to manage. The caller of a `CoffeeMachine::brew()` operation should not have to know how water is heated or beans are ground.

The quality of an abstraction depends on its boundary. If the interface exposes too many implementation details, clients become coupled to internal choices. If it hides information that callers genuinely need, the abstraction becomes frustrating or forces awkward workarounds. A stable abstraction therefore provides the smallest useful interface while preserving important guarantees.

Abstraction and encapsulation are related but not identical. Abstraction emphasizes what the user needs to know, while encapsulation emphasizes controlling access to state and behavior. A class can provide abstraction through a few public methods and use private helpers to implement them. When the internal representation changes but callers do not, the abstraction has successfully reduced coupling.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Design public APIs around useful capabilities and keep implementation details private.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain abstraction as hiding implementation details behind a useful contract. Distinguish abstraction from encapsulation and give an example where callers depend on behavior rather than storage.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Hiding everything without exposing a usable interface, designing abstractions around implementation details, and creating an abstraction before the domain has a real variation or invariant to protect.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A good abstraction minimizes the knowledge a caller needs. The implementation can change behind the boundary as long as the observable contract remains stable.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Consumers should depend on what an object does rather than how it stores or computes its state.
Avoid: Leaking representation details that callers then begin to depend upon.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A repository exposes `findCustomer()` rather than exposing its internal database connection and query construction.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: interfaces → encapsulation → information hiding → dependency inversion → API design.

topics.shortDescription: Understand abstraction as stable interfaces that hide implementation details and reduce unnecessary coupling.

topics.title: Data Encapsulation
topics.description: Learn encapsulation, private state, invariants, controlled mutation, and behavior-oriented class design.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Encapsulation is about keeping state and the operations that protect that state together while controlling how external code can change it. Private members are useful because they prevent callers from directly creating invalid combinations of state.

A setter for every private field is not automatically encapsulation. If a value has business rules, an operation that expresses the rule is usually stronger. For example, `withdraw(amount)` can reject an invalid amount and enforce balance constraints, while a public `setBalance()` would bypass the intended invariant.

Abstraction and encapsulation overlap but answer different questions. Abstraction asks what the user needs to know; encapsulation asks how state and behavior are packaged and protected.

Encapsulation is valuable when a type must protect an invariant. An invariant is a rule that should remain true for a valid object, such as a balance that cannot become negative under a particular business policy or a temperature setting that must stay within an accepted range. If every field is public, any caller can potentially violate that rule.

A common weak design is to make fields private but expose unrestricted setters for every field. This technically restricts direct access but may not protect the domain rules. Behavior-oriented methods are often stronger because they can validate the requested operation before changing state. For example, `withdraw(amount)` can reject an invalid withdrawal instead of allowing callers to assign an arbitrary balance.

Encapsulation also makes future changes safer. If the representation of a class changes, callers that depend only on the public behavior can remain unchanged. This is one reason classes are useful beyond simply grouping variables. They establish a controlled boundary around state and define how other parts of the program are allowed to interact with it.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Protect important invariants with behavior-oriented methods instead of unrestricted setters.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain encapsulation as controlling access to representation and preserving invariants. Compare public, protected, and private members and discuss why getters/setters are not automatically good encapsulation.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Making every field private but exposing unrestricted setters, leaking internal containers by reference, and confusing syntactic access control with a well-designed invariant.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Encapsulation is about controlling state transitions, not merely hiding fields. A class should expose operations that preserve valid state rather than giving callers unrestricted mutation.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: A class must protect invariants and control how state changes.
Avoid: Public mutable fields when unrestricted changes could create invalid states.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: An account object can validate withdrawals inside its API instead of allowing callers to directly assign an invalid balance.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: invariants → access control → abstraction → constructors → defensive programming.

topics.shortDescription: Learn encapsulation, private state, invariants, controlled mutation, and behavior-oriented class design.

topics.title: Interfaces
topics.description: Learn interface-like abstractions using pure virtual functions, dependency inversion, substitution, and focused capabilities.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
C++ has no dedicated `interface` keyword in the traditional sense. An interface-like design is commonly represented by an abstract class containing pure virtual functions and a virtual destructor.

The value of this pattern is dependency inversion. Code that needs to perform a payment can depend on a `PaymentGateway` capability instead of knowing whether the implementation uses a wallet, card provider, or test fake.

Small interfaces are easier to implement and test. If one interface contains unrelated responsibilities, implementations may be forced to provide meaningless operations. Designing around focused capabilities keeps dependencies narrow.

An interface represents a capability that client code can depend on without depending on one implementation. C++ expresses interface-like designs commonly through abstract classes containing pure virtual functions. The important part is the contract: what operations exist, what their inputs mean, and what behavior callers can rely on.

A small interface is easier to implement, test, and replace. For example, a payment consumer can depend on a `PaymentGateway` abstraction while production uses one gateway and tests use a fake implementation. This reduces the need for tests to perform real external operations.

Interface design should also consider ownership and lifetime. If a method receives a pointer, reference, or smart pointer, the interface should make it clear whether null is allowed and who owns the object. Virtual destructors matter for polymorphic interfaces because implementations may be destroyed through a base pointer. Good interfaces depend on stable capabilities rather than leaking internal implementation details.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use small abstract interfaces to reduce coupling and make alternative implementations testable.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain interface-like design in C++ using abstract classes and pure virtual functions. Discuss virtual dispatch, ownership of interface objects, and the importance of a virtual destructor in polymorphic bases.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Treating a class with unrelated implementation state as a pure interface, forgetting `const` consistency in overrides, and creating interfaces with too many methods.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: An interface is a promise about capabilities, not a promise about representation. Keep it small and stable so implementations can vary without forcing clients to understand their internals.

topics.shortDescription: Learn interface-like abstractions using pure virtual functions, dependency inversion, substitution, and focused capabilities.

modules.title: Files, Exceptions and Memory
modules.description: Learn files, exceptions and memory through explanations, examples, and practical exercises.

topics.title: Files And Streams
topics.description: Learn C++ file streams, reading, writing, persistence, open modes, failure handling, and RAII-based resource management.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
File streams connect C++ programs to persistent storage. `std::ifstream` is commonly used for reading, `std::ofstream` for writing, and `std::fstream` when both directions are required.

Opening a file is a fallible operation. A program should check the stream state before assuming the file is usable. It should also distinguish between replacing existing content and adding new content because the chosen open mode changes the file's behavior.

RAII makes file handling safer: a stream object owns the open resource for its lifetime and releases it automatically when it leaves scope. This is an important example of a broader C++ principle: resource cleanup should be attached to object lifetime whenever practical.

File streams are objects that connect program operations to persistent storage. `ifstream` is primarily for reading, `ofstream` for writing, and `fstream` supports both. Opening a stream can fail, so a program should treat successful construction/opening as a condition to verify rather than assuming the file is available.

RAII is especially useful for files. The stream object's lifetime controls the resource, so when the object leaves scope its destructor closes the underlying stream. This reduces the chance of forgetting cleanup on an error path. The same principle applies to other resources such as locks and dynamically acquired handles.

Text files are human-readable and convenient for simple records, but their format must be defined if the program will read the data later. Binary files preserve bytes directly but introduce portability and representation concerns. For either form, handle malformed data and I/O failures deliberately. A robust file operation is not simply 'open, read, close'; it defines what happens when opening fails, input is incomplete, storage is unavailable, or the data does not match the expected format.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Practice reading and writing files while handling missing files, malformed data, and resource lifetime.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain file streams, open modes, stream state, buffering at a high level, binary versus text concerns, and RAII-based closing. Be prepared to discuss checking both open and read/write success.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Assuming `open()` success means every later read will succeed, forgetting to validate output operations, mishandling binary data as text, and relying on manual `close()` for correctness instead of RAII.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: File I/O is interaction with an external resource and therefore can fail. Treat the stream object as the resource owner and check state at meaningful boundaries rather than assuming the filesystem behaves like memory.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:

topics.title: Exception Handling
topics.description: Understand throw, try, catch, standard exceptions, stack unwinding, and how RAII interacts with failures.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Exceptions provide a separate control path for failures that should not be handled as ordinary successful results. Code can `throw` an exception at the failure point and catch it at a level that knows how to respond.

The major benefit of exceptions in C++ is their interaction with object lifetime. During stack unwinding, local objects are destroyed, so RAII-managed resources are cleaned up even when execution leaves a scope unexpectedly.

Catch standard exceptions by `const` reference when appropriate. Avoid using exceptions as routine loop-control mechanisms. For expected outcomes that are frequent and ordinary, a status value or another explicit result representation can be clearer.

Exceptions provide a separate path for reporting failures that cannot be handled naturally at the immediate point of detection. `throw` transfers control, and a matching `catch` receives the exception. Catching standard exceptions by `const` reference avoids unnecessary copying and preserves polymorphic behavior.

The most important connection is between exceptions and RAII. During stack unwinding, local objects whose lifetimes end are destroyed automatically. If those objects own resources, their destructors can perform cleanup even when an exception interrupts normal control flow. This is why resource ownership should be represented by objects instead of scattered manual cleanup instructions.

Exceptions should communicate genuinely exceptional or failure conditions rather than ordinary branching. A parser may use a status value when invalid input is expected frequently, while a resource failure or violated precondition may justify an exception depending on the API design. Catch exceptions at a layer that can actually handle the failure. Catching everything too early and continuing can hide the original problem and leave the program in an invalid state.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use exceptions for exceptional failure paths and let RAII perform cleanup during stack unwinding.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain `try`, `throw`, `catch`, stack unwinding, exception safety, and RAII. Discuss the basic guarantees—no-throw, strong, and basic—and why cleanup should normally be automatic.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Catching everything and hiding errors, throwing from destructors, using exceptions for ordinary loop control, losing the original exception context, and managing resources manually across exception paths.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: An exception transfers control from the failure point to a matching handler while automatic objects in exited scopes are destroyed. RAII makes that unwinding safe because cleanup is tied to object lifetime.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: A failure cannot be handled meaningfully at the point where it occurs and should propagate to a layer that can recover or report it.
Avoid: Using exceptions for ordinary expected branching or throwing from destructors during stack unwinding.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A resource-opening function can throw a meaningful exception while RAII ensures already-acquired resources are cleaned up as the failure propagates.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: stack unwinding → RAII → `noexcept` → exception-safety guarantees → error/result types.

topics.title: Dynamic Memory
topics.description: Learn dynamic allocation, new/delete, smart pointers, ownership, lifetime, leaks, and why RAII is preferred.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Dynamic memory allows storage to be created at runtime and to outlive the scope in which the allocation request was made. Traditional C++ provides `new` and `delete`, including separate forms for arrays.

The critical rule is matching ownership and lifetime. Memory obtained with `new` must be released correctly, and array allocation must use the corresponding array deletion form. Failure to follow these rules can produce leaks, invalid deletion, or use-after-free bugs.

Modern C++ generally prefers RAII abstractions. `std::make_unique` expresses exclusive ownership, while containers such as `std::vector` manage dynamic sequences without requiring the programmer to manually call `delete`. Manual allocation is still relevant for low-level code, but it should be justified rather than used by default.

Dynamic memory exists because some objects need storage whose size or lifetime cannot conveniently be determined at compile time. `new` creates an object dynamically and `delete` releases it; arrays allocated with `new[]` require `delete[]`. Mismatching these forms is incorrect because the allocation and deallocation mechanisms must correspond.

The harder problem is ownership. A raw pointer does not by itself tell you who is responsible for deletion, how long the object remains alive, or whether multiple pointers refer to the same resource. This ambiguity produces leaks, double deletion, and use-after-free bugs. Modern C++ addresses this by expressing ownership with RAII types such as `std::unique_ptr` and `std::shared_ptr`.

For collections, `std::vector` should usually be preferred over manual dynamic arrays because it manages capacity, lifetime, and element destruction automatically. Manual allocation is still worth learning because it explains how ownership works and is required for some low-level interfaces. Whenever dynamic storage appears, immediately ask: who owns it, when does ownership begin, what happens if an operation fails, and exactly when is it released?

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Prefer RAII containers and smart pointers over manual `new`/`delete` in ordinary application code.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain dynamic storage, `new`/`delete`, ownership, memory leaks, dangling pointers, and why RAII/smart pointers are preferred. Compare `unique_ptr` and `shared_ptr` conceptually.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Mismatched `new[]`/`delete`, double deletion, leaked allocations, storing raw owning pointers, and creating reference cycles with `shared_ptr` without using `weak_ptr` where appropriate.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Dynamic allocation is a lifetime decision. Ask who owns the allocation and what event releases it. Modern C++ usually moves that responsibility into a resource-owning object so cleanup occurs automatically.

topics.title: Namespaces
topics.description: Understand namespaces, qualified names, using declarations, name collisions, and organization of larger codebases.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Namespaces provide a naming boundary so unrelated components can use similar names without colliding. A namespace-qualified name makes ownership of an identifier explicit.

For example, `inventory::findProduct()` communicates that the function belongs to the inventory domain. This is especially useful in large projects and when integrating third-party libraries.

A `using` declaration can bring one selected name into scope, while a broad `using namespace` directive can expose many names and increase collision risk. Broad directives are particularly undesirable in header files because they affect every source file that includes the header.

Namespaces organize names so unrelated components can use descriptive identifiers without colliding. A namespace is not a runtime container; it is primarily a compile-time naming mechanism. `billing::tax` clearly identifies which `tax` function is intended and makes large codebases easier to navigate.

Nested namespaces can express a hierarchy, and modern C++ supports compact nested namespace syntax. A using declaration can bring one specific name into scope, while a using directive can introduce many names. Broad using directives are especially risky in header files because they affect every source file that includes that header and can create unexpected ambiguities.

Namespaces also help separate public API from implementation details. A library can expose a documented namespace for consumers while keeping internal helpers in an implementation-oriented namespace. Combine namespaces with classes, modules/source files, and clear interfaces rather than using global variables as a substitute for organization. The goal is not merely avoiding duplicate names; it is making ownership of an API and the meaning of each identifier obvious.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use namespaces to make ownership of names explicit and reduce collisions in larger systems.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain namespaces, qualified names, `using` declarations, and anonymous namespaces/internal linkage at a high level. Discuss why namespaces prevent naming collisions in large programs.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Putting `using namespace std;` in public headers, creating broad `using` directives that cause ambiguity, and treating namespaces as runtime containers rather than compile-time name organization.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A namespace gives names a qualification context. It is primarily a way to organize interfaces and control collisions across a large program and multiple libraries.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Organizing APIs and preventing identifier collisions across libraries and application domains.
Avoid: Broad `using namespace` directives in headers.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A library can expose `billing::Invoice` while keeping implementation helpers in a private namespace, reducing accidental coupling.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: linkage → translation units → modules → qualified names → API organization.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Storage must outlive a scope or have a runtime-determined size and automatic/value storage is insufficient.
Avoid: Manual `new`/`delete` when an owning standard container or smart pointer can express the same design.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: `std::make_unique` expresses exclusive ownership and automatically releases the object, eliminating a large class of leak and double-delete bugs.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: ownership → RAII → `unique_ptr` → `shared_ptr` → allocators → move semantics.

topics.title: Templates
topics.description: Learn function and class templates, generic programming, type requirements, instantiation, and modern template design.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Templates let C++ express algorithms and data structures in terms of operations and types rather than one concrete type. A function template can compare two values without writing separate implementations for integers, floating-point values, or other compatible types.

The compiler generally generates a specialization when the template is used with a particular set of template arguments. This means generic code can remain strongly typed and can often be optimized without runtime type dispatch.

A useful template-design question is: what operations does the algorithm actually require? Modern C++ concepts can make those requirements explicit. Good generic code is not code that accepts absolutely anything; it is code whose required capabilities are clear and correctly constrained.

Templates allow one piece of code to describe an algorithm or type in terms of requirements rather than one concrete data type. A function template such as `larger` can work with integers, floating-point values, or user-defined types as long as the required comparison operation is valid.

Template code is generally instantiated when the compiler needs a concrete specialization. This provides compile-time type checking and often allows the compiler to optimize aggressively. The trade-off is that template diagnostics can become complex when the required operations are not available or when several conversions interact.

Generic programming becomes clearer when you think in terms of capabilities. Instead of asking 'what type is this?', ask 'what operations must this type support?' Modern C++ concepts can express such requirements more clearly. Templates are also the foundation of standard containers such as `std::vector<T>` and algorithms that operate over ranges. Use templates when the same behavior genuinely applies to multiple types; do not introduce templates simply to make a small piece of code look more abstract.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Write generic algorithms around the operations they actually require.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain function/class templates, type deduction, instantiation, specialization at a high level, and compile-time polymorphism. Mention concepts when discussing modern C++ constraints.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Writing unconstrained templates with unreadable diagnostics, putting required template definitions where they cannot be instantiated, and assuming templates are runtime generic objects rather than compile-time machinery.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A template is a pattern from which the compiler can generate code for specific types or values. Generic design works best when the required operations and constraints are explicit.

topics.title: Preprocessor
topics.description: Understand preprocessing, includes, macros, conditional compilation, include guards, and safer modern alternatives.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
The preprocessor performs textual and conditional processing before normal C++ compilation. It handles directives such as `#include`, `#define`, and conditional compilation.

Macros are powerful but bypass many normal language checks because substitution happens before the compiler sees the final C++ expression. A function-like macro can therefore evaluate an argument more than once, creating bugs when the argument has side effects.

Prefer typed C++ facilities such as `constexpr`, inline functions, templates, and normal constants when they express the requirement. The preprocessor remains useful for include guards, platform-specific compilation, and build configuration, but modern C++ usually keeps macro logic small and localized.

The preprocessor operates before the main C++ compilation stage. It handles directives such as `#include`, macro definitions, and conditional compilation. Because macros are textual substitutions, they do not behave like typed variables or functions and can create problems that ordinary C++ expressions would prevent.

For example, a macro can accidentally evaluate an argument more than once, interact strangely with operator precedence, or expose names globally within the translation unit. Prefer `constexpr` for named compile-time values, inline functions for ordinary computations, and templates for generic behavior when those features express the requirement better.

Conditional compilation remains useful for platform-specific code and build configurations. Header inclusion also requires protection against repeated inclusion, commonly through include guards or supported alternatives. The most useful mental model is that preprocessor output becomes input to the compiler. If a macro or conditional directive changes the source before compilation, the compiler can only diagnose the resulting program. Keeping preprocessing simple makes the actual C++ easier to reason about.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Use macros only where preprocessing is genuinely required; prefer typed C++ alternatives otherwise.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain macro expansion, `#include`, conditional compilation, include guards, and why `constexpr`, inline functions, templates, and language features often provide safer alternatives to function-like macros.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Macro side effects, missing parentheses in macro definitions, multiple evaluation of arguments, global macro name collisions, and relying on conditional compilation where normal language abstractions would be clearer.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Preprocessing happens before ordinary C++ compilation. It performs textual transformations rather than type-aware C++ operations, which is why macros can bypass the safety and scope rules of normal language constructs.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Conditional compilation, include guards, or controlled source-level configuration is genuinely required.
Avoid: Function-like macros when an inline function, constexpr value, enum, template, or language feature can provide type-safe behavior.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: Platform-specific integration may require conditional compilation, but ordinary business logic should remain in C++ rather than macro branches.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: translation phases → macros → include guards → conditional compilation → templates.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: The same algorithm or type relationship should work across different types while preserving compile-time checking and performance.
Avoid: Templates whose abstraction is less clear than a simple concrete function or runtime interface.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A generic sorting or transformation utility can work for multiple value types without virtual dispatch, while concepts can constrain the operations required.

sections.title: Related concepts

topics.title: Signal Handling
topics.description: Learn the fundamentals and limitations of asynchronous process signals and safe signal-handling patterns.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Signals are asynchronous notifications delivered to a process. That makes them fundamentally different from an ordinary function call: a signal can arrive at a point in execution that the program did not explicitly request.

Signal handlers therefore have strict constraints. Complex operations, allocation, and arbitrary library calls should not be performed casually from a handler. A safer pattern is to record a minimal notification and let the normal program flow perform cleanup and shutdown.

The important learning goal is to understand the boundary between asynchronous notification and ordinary program logic. Treating a signal handler as a normal callback can introduce subtle correctness problems.

Signals are different from ordinary function calls because they can arrive asynchronously relative to the program's normal control flow. A signal handler may interrupt execution at a point where many library operations or application invariants are not safe to manipulate. This is why signal handlers should perform only carefully permitted, minimal work.

A common design is to record a simple shutdown request and let the normal execution path notice it. The main loop can then close files, release resources, stop worker threads, and perform other ordinary cleanup in a controlled context. Trying to perform complex cleanup directly inside an asynchronous handler can introduce subtle problems.

Signal behavior can also vary by platform and signal type, so portable code should rely only on guarantees that apply to the environment being targeted. For learning, focus first on the distinction between asynchronous notification and normal function invocation. Once that distinction is clear, the restrictions on what a handler should do become much easier to understand.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Keep signal handling minimal and let ordinary program flow perform cleanup and shutdown.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain what a signal represents, why handlers have severe restrictions, and why complex work should not normally be performed directly inside an asynchronous signal handler. Distinguish process termination signals from application-level error handling.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Calling non-signal-safe library functions from a handler, assuming every signal can be caught or ignored, using signals as a general-purpose thread synchronization mechanism, and performing complex allocation or I/O from a handler.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A signal is an asynchronous notification that can interrupt normal execution. Because it may arrive at an unexpected point, the safe handler work is deliberately limited; communicate the event to normal program flow instead of doing substantial work inside the handler.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Responding to process-level asynchronous notifications within the narrow guarantees provided by the platform and language.
Avoid: Performing complex work, allocating memory, locking mutexes, or calling arbitrary non-async-signal-safe functions inside a signal handler.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A handler may set a simple flag of suitable type, with the main execution path performing orderly shutdown and cleanup.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: asynchronous execution → atomics → process lifecycle → shutdown coordination → OS signals.

topics.title: Multithreading
topics.description: Understand threads, joining, atomics, mutexes, races, deadlocks, synchronization, and concurrency design.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Multithreading allows independent execution flows to run concurrently. `std::thread` can start a function on another thread, and `join()` waits for that thread to finish.

The difficult part is shared state. If two threads modify the same object without appropriate synchronization, the program can contain a data race and therefore have undefined behavior. A mutex can protect a critical section, while atomics are useful for certain individual shared values when their semantics are sufficient.

Concurrency also introduces deadlocks, starvation, contention, and lifetime problems. Keep critical sections small, make ownership explicit, and prefer immutable data or message-passing designs when they reduce synchronization requirements.

A thread is an independent path of execution within a process, but threads share many resources. That sharing is powerful because threads can cooperate on common data, but it creates synchronization requirements whenever mutable state can be accessed concurrently.

A data race occurs when conflicting accesses happen without the synchronization required by the language. The result is not merely 'one thread wins'; unsynchronized access can produce undefined behavior. A mutex creates a critical section in which related operations are protected. `std::lock_guard` and `std::scoped_lock` use RAII so the lock is released automatically when the guard leaves scope.

`join()` establishes that the creating thread waits for completion. Detached threads require much more careful lifetime reasoning because the creator no longer has the same direct synchronization relationship with the thread. Modern C++ also provides atomics, condition variables, futures, and task-oriented facilities. Prefer the simplest concurrency model that solves the problem, keep shared mutable state small, and make ownership and shutdown behavior explicit.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Practice concurrency by identifying shared state first, then choosing atomics, mutexes, or message passing.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain thread creation, join versus detach, shared-state races, mutexes, locks, atomics, condition variables, and deadlock at a conceptual level. Be ready to distinguish a data race from ordinary logical contention.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Accessing shared non-atomic data without synchronization, forgetting to join a joinable thread, holding locks while calling unknown code, acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order, and assuming `volatile` provides thread safety.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: Concurrency is primarily an ownership and synchronization problem. Decide which state is shared, who may mutate it, what establishes happens-before relationships, and how thread lifetime is managed before choosing a primitive.

topics.shortDescription: Understand threads, joining, atomics, mutexes, races, deadlocks, synchronization, and concurrency design.

topics.title: Web Programming
topics.description: Learn C++ web-programming fundamentals through HTTP/CGI concepts, request handling, validation, and security boundaries.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
C++ can participate in web systems at several levels, from low-level HTTP handling to modern framework or service implementations. The supplied material focuses on the older CGI model, which is useful for learning how a web server can invoke a program and provide request information.

The durable concepts are the HTTP request/response model, headers, request methods, query/body data, cookies, and server-side validation. External input should always be treated as untrusted.

Security requirements are especially important around file uploads, paths, commands, authentication, and output encoding. Modern production C++ web systems commonly use HTTP libraries, frameworks, reverse proxies, and structured service architectures rather than implementing a complete web stack manually.

The supplied material uses CGI as the historical model for connecting a C++ program to a web server. Although modern applications more commonly use frameworks, HTTP libraries, or service architectures, the underlying concepts remain useful. A request contains a method, target information, headers, and possibly a body; the response contains status information, headers, and a body.

GET and POST should not be thought of merely as two different ways to submit a form. They have different semantics and are used differently by clients, caches, and servers. Cookies can associate small pieces of state with a client, but they should never be treated as inherently trustworthy input.

Security is part of web programming from the beginning. External input must be validated, output must be encoded appropriately, uploaded files must be constrained, and file paths must not be accepted blindly from users. Authentication and authorization answer different questions: who is the caller, and what is that caller allowed to do? Even when using a modern framework, these underlying concepts remain essential.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Learn HTTP fundamentals and treat all external request data as untrusted.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain the request/response model, HTTP methods, status codes, headers, URL structure, and the difference between a client and server. For C++, discuss that networking is usually provided through libraries or frameworks rather than the standard language alone.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Treating HTTP as a reliable stateful connection, putting secrets in URLs, ignoring status codes, trusting client input, and confusing transport security with application authorization.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: A web interaction is a protocol boundary. The client sends a request containing method, target, headers, and possibly a body; the server validates it, performs application logic, and returns a response whose status, headers, and body communicate the result.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Building or integrating C++ services that communicate over HTTP or another network protocol.
Avoid: Treating CGI as the default modern architecture; it is useful historically and conceptually, while production systems commonly use HTTP libraries/frameworks and reverse proxies.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A C++ service validates request input, authenticates the caller, authorizes the operation, performs business logic, and returns a correctly formed response without trusting client-supplied data.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: HTTP semantics → serialization → authentication → authorization → input validation → TLS → REST/RPC.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Independent work can execute concurrently and the synchronization cost is justified by the workload.
Avoid: Sharing mutable state casually; concurrency adds correctness obligations as well as performance opportunities.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A worker pool can process jobs from a synchronized queue, with explicit ownership, cancellation, and shutdown behavior.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: data races → mutexes → atomics → condition variables → futures → memory ordering → deadlock.

topics.title: Stl Tutorial
topics.description: Master the STL mental model of containers, iterators, algorithms, ranges, and choosing appropriate standard containers.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
The STL is built around a powerful separation of responsibilities: containers manage collections, iterators describe positions or ranges, and algorithms operate on those ranges.

A `std::vector` is often a strong default sequence container because its elements are contiguous and it works efficiently with many algorithms. Other containers exist because different access, insertion, ordering, or lookup requirements call for different trade-offs.

The important shift is to think in terms of operations rather than hand-written loops. If `std::sort`, `std::find`, `std::count`, or another standard algorithm expresses the intent directly, using it usually makes the program shorter and easier to verify.

The STL is easiest to learn as a relationship among containers, iterators, and algorithms. A container manages a collection of objects, an iterator identifies positions or ranges within that collection, and an algorithm performs an operation over an iterator range. This separation allows the same algorithm to work with many different containers.

`std::vector` is often a strong default sequence container because its elements are contiguous and it provides efficient iteration and random access. `std::list` and `std::deque` have different structural properties, while associative containers such as `map` and `set` organize data around keys and ordering. Unordered containers use hashing and provide different performance characteristics.

Algorithms such as `sort`, `find`, `count`, and transformations often express intent more clearly than custom loops. Iterator invalidation is an important advanced topic: operations that change a container can invalidate iterators or references to its elements. Learn not only which container to choose, but also what happens to references and iterators when the container changes.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Learn containers, iterators, and algorithms as one connected STL model.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Know the major STL families: containers, iterators, algorithms, function objects, and utilities. Explain why algorithms are written against iterator/range abstractions and how container choice affects complexity.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Choosing containers only by habit, invalidating iterators or references after container modification, using linear-search containers for frequent key lookup, and ignoring algorithmic complexity.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: STL design separates data representation from operations. A container owns or organizes data, iterators/ranges describe traversal, and algorithms perform reusable work over that traversal model.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: Solving collection-processing problems with standard containers, iterators, algorithms, and ranges rather than hand-written data-structure code.
Avoid: Choosing containers without considering complexity, memory locality, or iterator invalidation.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: A vector plus standard algorithms is often simpler and faster than a custom collection for ordinary sequence processing; use associative containers when lookup semantics justify them.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: containers → iterators → algorithms → ranges → complexity → iterator invalidation.

topics.title: Standard Library
topics.description: Explore major C++ standard-library facilities and learn when to reuse library components instead of building custom solutions.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
The C++ standard library is a collection of reusable facilities rather than a single monolithic feature. It covers input/output, strings, containers, algorithms, memory management, time, random generation, exceptions, utilities, and more.

A productive C++ developer learns to search the standard library before implementing common functionality from scratch. Using `std::vector` instead of a custom dynamic array, `std::sort` instead of a hand-written sorting routine, or `std::unique_ptr` instead of manual ownership can eliminate entire categories of bugs.

The standard library also provides consistent interfaces. Once you understand concepts such as iterators, ranges, RAII, callable objects, and value semantics, many seemingly different facilities start to feel like variations of the same design patterns.

The standard library is a major part of practical C++ because it provides tested building blocks for common tasks. Instead of implementing a dynamic array, string abstraction, sorting routine, hash table, smart pointer, or file stream from scratch, use the standard facility when it matches the requirement.

Learning the library also teaches modern C++ design. `std::vector` demonstrates managed dynamic storage, `std::string` manages text, `<algorithm>` provides reusable operations, `<memory>` provides ownership abstractions, `<chrono>` models time, and `<random>` separates engines from distributions. These facilities reinforce a consistent principle: resource management and common behavior should be expressed through reusable types and algorithms.

A practical learning habit is to recognize a problem before writing code. If you need a growable sequence, investigate `vector`; if you need key/value lookup, investigate `map` or `unordered_map`; if you need sorting, investigate `<algorithm>`; if you need exclusive ownership, investigate `unique_ptr`. Using the standard library reduces custom code and gives future readers familiar abstractions.

sections.title: Example
Practical use
sections.content: Before writing custom infrastructure, check whether the standard library already provides a reliable solution.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain that the C++ standard library is a collection of standardized facilities for strings, containers, algorithms, memory management, I/O, concurrency, time, and more. Be ready to justify using a standard facility instead of custom infrastructure.

sections.title: Common pitfalls
sections.content: Common pitfalls: Reimplementing standard algorithms, assuming all library operations have the same complexity, ignoring iterator invalidation rules, and using low-level facilities when a safer standard abstraction already expresses the requirement.

sections.title: Deep mental model
sections.content: Deep mental model: The standard library is part of the C++ programming model, not an optional toolbox. Learn to recognize common requirements—ownership, sequence storage, lookup, transformation, synchronization, time, and I/O—and map them to established facilities.

sections.title: When to use and when to avoid
sections.content:
Use it when: A standard facility already provides the required abstraction, algorithm, container, utility, or resource management behavior.
Avoid: Reimplementing mature standard facilities without a concrete requirement.

sections.title: Production scenario
sections.content: Production scenario: Prefer standard strings, containers, smart pointers, algorithms, chrono utilities, and concurrency primitives before introducing custom equivalents.

sections.title: Related concepts
sections.content: Related concepts: STL → RAII → algorithms → containers → smart pointers → `<chrono>` → `<thread>`

topics.shortDescription: Explore major C++ standard-library facilities and learn when to reuse library components instead of building custom solutions.
